chapter_theme: An envoy must combine love, knowledge, learning and presence with exact speech, courage and incorruptibility, and must carry his sovereign's interest to a foreign court even at the cost of his life.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: qualities common to both kinds of envoy (681-682), the envoy who composes his own message (683-687), and the one who repeats the message as given (688-690). He relates this to a Sanskrit grading of envoys as highest, middle and lowest.

681.reading: Love, birth in an honourable family, and qualities kings desire make up the nature of one who carries a message.
681.nuance: Whatever அன்பு means here, the envoy's list begins from the affections, not the skills. Parimelazhagar's 'qualities kings desire' also serve abroad: foreign kings too come under his sway.

positions.position: The love is for one's own kin, which keeps them from harm, and the birth is in a family fit for ministry.
The love is for the king, and 'qualities kings desire' means not desiring what the king desires.
positions.quote: வேந்தனால் விரும்பப்படும் குணமுடைமையாவது அவன் விரும்புவனவற் றைத் தான் விரும்பாமை.

682.reading: Love, knowledge and carefully considered eloquence are the three things an envoy can't do without.
682.nuance: ஆராய்ந்த qualifies eloquence, and Parimelazhagar takes it as choosing words that will win assent. Parimelazhagar reads this verse's love as being for the king, so he has given the two adjacent verses two different objects of love.

683.reading: It is the mark of one who speaks of victory among spear-bearers to be strong in the treatises among those who know them.
683.nuance: The two audiences are set side by side: those with treatises and those with spears. Parimelazhagar sharpens the first: the ministers there merely understand the texts, while the envoy must be able to set them out.

684.reading: Let one who has these three together go on this work: understanding, presence and well-tested learning.
684.nuance: உரு, bodily presence, counts as a requirement. Parimelazhagar says all three earn respect, on which the work depends, and that such a combination in one person is rare.

685.reading: The envoy is one who speaks in brief, removes what would offend, speaks so as to bring a smile, and thereby gets good done.
685.nuance: Parimelazhagar gives each tactic a psychology: when told a compressed reason, hearers who would refuse many matters come round; when told in a pleasing way, they accept hard things without noticing they are hard. Courtesy is presented as technique.

686.reading: The envoy is one who is learned, does not fear hostile eyes, speaks so that it goes home, and knows what fits the time.
686.nuance: Parimelazhagar notes that காலத்தால் தக்கது allows for ends reached by means other than what the treatises taught. Manakkudavar makes the learning very specific: how to turn aside the enemy king's anger.

687.reading: The highest is the one who knows the protocol, considers the moment, knows the place, and speaks after thinking it through.
687.nuance: Parimelazhagar's எண்ணி is rehearsal in chains: what I say, what they answer, what I say next. His இடம் is a place where one's allies are present, so a place is political, not physical.

688.reading: Purity, support, resolve and truthfulness in these three mark the one who delivers the message faithfully.
688.nuance: Parimelazhagar's purity is immunity to bribes of money and women, so that the message isn't altered. Truth here is a qualification for being believed. These are professional virtues as he explains them, not an inner holiness.

positions.position: துணைமை is having the foreign court's ministers as support, which can calm a king's anger.
துணைமை is having one's own retinue, and purity is of body and mind.

689.reading: One who conveys the king's reply to kings is a hard man whose mouth will not let slip a word that shames.
689.nuance: வன்கண் is again a virtue, as in 632, and Parimelazhagar shows why: the temptation comes from fear for oneself. The slip would be a phrase softening his king's standing in order to save his skin.

690.reading: The envoy is one who, even if it brings his end, doesn't hold back and secures what is good for his lord.
690.nuance: இறுதி is the limit, and the chapter stops there. The ideal is unconditional, and the verse gives no reason why the envoy should owe so much; it's taken for granted.

links.note: Two agents of the king, both ready for death, with opposite methods: the spy says nothing whatever is done to him (586), and the envoy says everything whatever may come (690). They share an unflinching eye: compare 585's கண்ணஞ்சாது with 686's கண் அஞ்சான்.

667 says never to scorn anyone for their form. 684 makes form (உரு) one of three requirements of the envoy. Parimelazhagar's explanation is that foreign courts respect the look of a man. The Kural is apparently distinguishing what people should do from what they in fact do.

source_issues: 686: Kalaignar's text starts with a stray fragment of the verse and a number (தக்க தறிவதாந் தூது. 686) before the commentary.
687: Manakkudavar's commentary is marked as not aligned. Parimelazhagar's text reads உரைப்பான் தரை for தலை.
